references.text: The Lord says that the sin of Sodom and Gomorrah is so great that he must go down to see whether what they have done is truly as bad as the outcry against them has reached him, which points to the great wickedness in these cities.
The inhabitants of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand to have sexual relations with the two angels who have come to the city, illustrating the depth of their evil.
The Lord causes sulfur and fire to rain down on Sodom and Gomorrah as punishment for their sins, confirming the description of the great wickedness of its inhabitants.
There is a warning against following the way of Sodom and Gomorrah, which refers back to their sinfulness and the punishment they received.
The Lord compares the leaders and people of Jerusalem with Sodom and Gomorrah because of their rebellion against him, reflecting the same kind of evil.
The prophet Ezekiel explicitly describes Sodom's sins: pride, abundance, and carelessness; they did not help the poor and needy but acted abominably before the Lord.
Peter refers to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of God's judgment, describing how the righteous Lot was tormented by the lawless people's depraved lives.
Jude mentions Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire because of sexual immorality and unnatural desires.
The great city, where their Lord was crucified, is compared to Sodom, pointing to deep-seated evil and rejection of God's ways.
Both verses illustrate how contempt for God leads to a sin that is 'great' and grievous in the Lord's eyes.
Isaiah uses Sodom as a direct theological image to describe the open and unforgivable sin in Jerusalem.
Jeremiah identifies Jerusalem's leaders as 'like Sodom,' giving deeper understanding of Sodom's nature as a symbol of total moral decay.
The description of Israel's decline in Isaiah 1:4 mirrors the moral condition of Sodom, both characterized by having abandoned and despised God.
